articles.headline: The Past, Present, and Future of Persona with P-Studio Head Kazuhisa Wada | IGN30 Interview
keyFacts: Kazuhisa Wada explained that Atlus developer fate depended on the success of Persona 3 during the mid-2000s.
Wada stated that Persona 4 Arena began as a fighting game idea he and Shigenori Soejima discussed during lunch breaks.
Wada said that giving younger developers a voice in the direction of Persona is important for carrying its legacy.
body: From Persona 2: Eternal Punishment to the upcoming Persona 6, creative producer and chief director of P-Studio with Atlus Kazuhisa Wada has had a hand in shaping the spinoff-turned-mainline series. And with the career spanning over 30 years, we're excited to see how he and his team continue to shape the beloved RPG series. As part of our IGN30 series where we have open conversations with storied developers about their careers from the early days to where they are today, I talked with Wada-san and he shared anecdotes of coming up through Atlus' ranks and what he envisions for the future of the franchise.

The advent of 3D graphics and making in-game events got him a jumpstart with games such as Maken X and the beloved Shin Megami Tensei 3: Nocturne – however, he explained that Atlus' fate hung in the balance of Persona 3's success back in the mid-2000s. The series' rise in popularity led to spinoffs as well, which sparked by spending lunch breaks playing fighting games with Shigenori Soejima, eventually leading to Persona 4 Arena. But now with a new numbered entry on the horizon and leading the development team, Wada-san says that giving younger developers a say in the direction and identity of Persona is important for carrying its legacy for generations to come. Here's our conversation about all that and more.
This interview was conducted with Sega interpreter Gavin Green and was edited for clarity and readability. You can watch the video version of this interview above.
IGN: I want to go back to your origins – tell me about the early years of being a game developer and working with Atlus.

Kazuhisa Wada: One of the reasons I wanted to join the games industry was that I grew up with games, I was there to watch the evolution. When I was in elementary school, there were things like Game & Watch, and as I grew older, eventually the Famicom, the NES, and then the Super NES and Super Famicom came out. And when I hit university, the PlayStation and the Saga Saturn came out. For me, that was a really big inspiration and throughout the entire time I stayed a gamer, it was kind of what made me want to join the game industry eventually. And one of the things that really hit the hardest for me was Shin Megami Tensei. It was because I encountered Shin Megami Tensei that I wanted to join Atlus. I was like, 'wow, this could be so cool.' Shin Megami Tensei really, really wowed me when I first saw it and said it had such a cool visual. And when I finally played the game, I was thinking it was really different in so many ways from so many games that I played before. The choices that you made really took you down all these very interesting paths and you got to explore this really fascinating story. So, it really inspired me and made me want to join Atlus.

Eventually, I was able to join Atlus and the very first game I was involved in was a game for the Dreamcast called Maken X. One of the things that actually got me into Atlus was the fact that it was the period where 3D graphics were just starting to come into vogue. I had never actually studied 3D graphics or graphic design, but it was this kind of new thing that had so much possibility. And I had essentially made my own 3D movie and I brought it to Atlus and said, 'Hey, here, this is what I can do. You want to hire me?' And they're like, 'Okay!" And Maken X was actually the very first game that [Katsura] Hashino-san was the director on.

Back then, I was part of the event team making cutscenes and the various things that were going to be in the [in-game] events, but we were not very big back then and the event team was very, very small. It was not like you could just only make events and that was all you needed to focus on. The era that we lived in was that, if you were a part of the event team, you didn't just make the events, you made every asset that went into the events. So it was a very, very stringent, tough situation. Yes, it was hard and they made me do all sorts of different things, but it taught me so much about game development. I got my hands on and did 3D models, character models, camera work with the events. It was really an incredible learning experience for me and Maken X really helped me grow as a creator overall.

IGN: Part of that journey was working with Katsura Hashino, Shoji Meguro, and Shigenori Soejima. With characters, music, art style, and stories that these games tell, I want to get your thoughts and your history working with them and pulling all these different pieces together to form a full game and what it was like to work with them.

KW: When I joined the company, Hashino-san and Meguro-san were like these senpais. They had been there for so long and I was starry-eyed within the company. Soejima-san was also kind of like that, but he's also much closer to me in age and we were much closer in terms of the work we did. We were both working on graphics and talking about how we wanted to realize various aspects of the art. We felt like we were working [together], we had a closer relationship to start with. This is kind of the era before he was focused on being a character designer. He was working on all aspects of game design, and as we mentioned before, it was the era where games were shifting into 3D.

Obviously he's an incredibly talented 2D artist, but he was doing less and less 2D art and focusing more on all sorts of other aspects of art and graphic design for games. Around this period, we had a chance to work on Shin Megami Tensei 3 together and we both actually worked on the opening sequences. I was in charge of the primary opening sequence and Soejima-san worked on the sub-opening sequence. We had a really close relationship, so we were kind of like, 'Okay, how do we want to develop differences between them? How do we want to make them different but similar?' It was very fun.

Outside of the opening, I worked on a lot of different aspects of that game with Meguro-san and everybody else as well. Some of the things I did was making the protagonist character model and working on a number of cutscenes and events. And there's this one event where when you died, [the camera] came overhead and angels swirled around you and brought you back to life. That was me. But it was also a really great opportunity to work with Meguro-san and hear his music first hand. My relationship with Meguro started when I was working on that opening movie I talked about. I got really cheeky and I was like, 'Hey, Meguro-san, this is the sort of music I want you to make. Make it for me.'

Then probably one of the major evolutions in my work at Atlus came with the creation of Persona 3. It was the first game where I worked in design and direction, and it was because Hashino-san had actually asked for me by name. And so it was with Persona 3 that we really hit upon this overall team setup where Soejima-san was working on character design and I was in charge leading the design of the game itself. Meguro-san was the sound composer and Hashino-san was the overall director. When we made Persona 3, it was not the best time for Atlus. There was a lot of talk that, 'Hey, if Persona 3 isn't a success, Atlus itself might no longer be able to continue game development.' Because we were in that situation, we all rolled up our sleeves and were like, 'Alright, we're going to try all sorts of crazy stuff to really make this game the best it could possibly be.'

If Persona 3 wasn't a success, Atlus itself might no longer be able to continue game development. The overall theme of the game, Hashino came up with the initial concept of it, but as a team, we all got together like, 'Alright, how do we want to work this? Where do we want to go with it?' It was really fun and way in the beginning, when we had the initial design of the game, we said, 'Okay, let's go work on the character design, let's come up with an image board.' So, I worked really closely with Soejima-san and we came up with a bunch of various images that would represent the feeling and the direction of the game. Then I remember we went to show it to Meguro-san to see what sort of music he'll come up with. And he got really inspired by it. He was like, "Okay, if you're going to bring this , I'm going to bring that ,' so there's this amazing almost session quality to it where one of us would do something that would inspire the next thing, and that would then inspire the next thing. It was like a stack of dominoes falling over. And that was the story of how Persona 3 came to be.

IGN: I always tell people that Persona 3 in my heart is my favorite, and that story really hits me really hard. And of course, Persona 4 Revival is coming soon which speaks to the popularity of Persona 4. But I kind of want to go back to Persona 5 and the moment that game came out, because that felt like the moment the series hit mass appeal and exploded in popularity. What was it like inside Atlus when Persona 5 first hit and took the world by storm?

KW: So for Persona 5, it wasn't a simultaneous release. We'd released the Japanese version initially and then there was a bit of a time gap between that and the worldwide edition. After we released the domestic [Japanese] edition, we actually got this feeling of, 'Oh wow, this game is getting popular. It seems to be well-received!' And then we had the worldwide release and the same thing happened, like, 'Wow, this is being very well-received!' But it wasn't really a surprise when it hit because we had this feeling, we had this inkling that maybe we got something here.

IGN: Persona 5 has had a lot of spinoffs, and the same thing goes for Persona 3 and 4. You've worked on a lot of the spinoffs in the Persona series, so I want to get an idea of the role of spinoffs play and why they're important and the philosophy behind doing spinoff games at Atlus.

KW: So, our very first spinoff was for Persona 4 – Persona 4 Arena. It was the first time we'd ever made a fighting game, it was the first time we'd ever worked with Arc System Works, and it was the first time we ever made a game for the arcade. A lot of new challenges, right? The success of that and the doing that really inspires us to then make more spinoffs in the future. But really, the reason why we did that was because we just wanted to try it. It just seemed like it would be really fun. The initial inspiration for making a fighting game spinoff of the Persona series was because at that time, Soejima-san and I were sitting next to each other in the office, and every day during lunch breaks, we'd just be like, 'Hey, you want to play some fighting games?' Then we'd just go battle each other. And so I was like, 'Hey man, what if we made Persona a fighting game? Would that be really interesting? That'd fit well.' And that was the entire impetus for it.

Of course, there were tons of other reasons why we ended up making spinoffs, but one of the major things that eventually became a consideration was the fact that between each numbered Persona, there ended up being several years between them. Games take a long time to make, so we wanted to make something that would keep the Persona momentum going and give fans something to do. We did this as a way to release Persona stuff regularly. One of the other advantages that we had when working on the spinoffs was that it gave us a chance to revisit a lot of the characters we loved from previous games and explore them and their personalities a little bit more. For both us and for the fans of those characters, it let us explore the world of Persona in a deeper and meaningful way.

IGN: Remasters and re-releases are also an important part of the Persona franchise. I want to get a little bit of the philosophy behind doing them and the role they have at Atlus. People love Persona 1 and Persona 2 and would love to see those stories modernized as well. How do you feel about working on remasters and why they're important?

KW: For me, I think remasters and remakes are really important just in general. I think they're a form of cultural preservation, right? We have these incredible games that, unless you bring to the modern day onto modern systems, might disappear from the world. And these are wonderful games. There are wonderful stories out there that can touch so many people's hearts, and we want to give them a chance to reach new players as well. So, this way of preserving them and giving them to another generation is really the importance of having remasters.

IGN: Now, I want to talk about the future of Persona. You have Persona 6 coming sometime in the future, but in your eyes, now that you are in charge of the direction of the series at P-Studio within Atlus: What do you feel like the series needs to do in order to keep growing and evolving?

KW: As you're all probably aware, games in the modern age take a long time to make. There are usually many years between games in a series, and games in general are on larger scales. It's kind of gotten to the point where you can no longer just have one or two people or a small team make a game at a major studio. So, one thing we really need to think about is, since this is no longer an individual kind of process and is more of a team situation, we want to make sure everybody at our company shares the basic vision for the future of Persona. Everybody gets to have a say. We get to share the direction we want to go in, get feedback, have conversations with everybody we're working with. And we want to make sure we bring in the younger generations of game developers into the process as well so that they have a voice and they have a way to show their own creative incredible-ness to the world.

We want to make sure we bring in the younger generations of game developers into the process as well so that they have a voice. Of course the Persona series that exists today is in thanks to many people who came before me, to people of my generation, and to people who are coming in the next generation as well. So, we really hope that the future of the Persona series is something that can continue onwards and that we can work with creators of the past, present, and future to continue making amazing games. The Persona that we've established, the identity of it, we hope to pass that identity, pass that Persona flame, to the next generation; let them understand the identity of it, but then let them give it their own spin and their own flavor and then pass that flame onto the next generation and keep it going so that the Persona series lasts for forever.

articles.headline: Incoming Rep. Anthony Constantino clarifies his comment on turning ‘every gay American’ into a Republican
keyFacts: Rep.-elect Anthony Constantino stated on social media that one of his top goals as a congressman is to make every gay American a Republican.
Constantino clarified in subsequent social media posts and interviews that he is not gay, stating his personal orientation is irrelevant to his political mission.
Constantino told The Post that the Republican Party delivers for gay Americans through policies like low taxes and safe streets while claiming Democrats endanger communities.
body: Outspoken Rep.-elect Anthony Constantino got personal online after announcing last week that he was driven to “get every gay American to be Republican.”
“I’m not Gay!” Constantino, 44, bluntly told his followers in a 2:30 a.m. X post on Friday after Thanksgiving.

The upstate NY Republican and Sticker Mule CEO, who credits his win this month to having “stood by” President Trump, drew public and media interest last week when he posted about his mission on social media.
Advertisement

“Now that I’m elected, one of my big goals is to get every gay American to be Republican,” Constantino pledged in a brief video from a moving vehicle posted to X on Sunday evening. He called it, “One of my top priorities as Congressman!”
His original post drew more than 700,000 views, and plenty of compliments, insults – and more than a few propositions.
“You’re really handsome,” wrote one user on X. “You turned me Republican,” wrote another.
Advertisement
He also posted a clip of a Newsmax interview, when anchor Greg Kelly asked him straight up: “Are you gay?”
“No,” Constantino replied. “But it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t really matter. It’s irrelevant.
“What matters is: I’m an ideological Republican. I think the Republican Party is for all people that believe what I believe.
Advertisement

“I want to champion American exceptionalism. I want to make us a nation where people can be successful. You know, gay people like making money,” he said. “They’re very successful at times. Why vote Democrat? They should be voting Republican.”
Constantino told The Post, “The Republican Party is delivering for gay Americans, while the Democratic Party is endangering gay communities.”
“I’m simply explaining why. I want low taxes, clean cities, safe streets, border security and prosperity,” he said.
Advertisement

“That’s why I advocate for employers to issue $1,000 Christmas bonuses and for data centers, which are job creating gold mines when built correctly, without using local water and by generating their own power,” he continued.

“Everything I advocate for benefits all Americans, including gay Americans. Meanwhile, Democrats prioritize illegal immigrants over Americans, dirty our cities, destroy local economies, and make us unsafe.”
Advertisement
He also reposted a comment by a self-described “trans Republican” who linked to Constantino’s own comment and called to “end the mutilation of children” and “no males in women’s spaces.”

Constantino posted a Thanksgiving message where he blasted Mayor Zohran Mamdani and advised: “To Conservatives who think being Gay is against God, remember that Jesus taught us not to judge and to Love Thy Neighbor.”

articles.headline: No elevation of lead detected in drinking water after detonations in Iowa, EPA says
keyFacts: The EPA stated that initial lab results showed no elevation of lead in drinking water sources after the Army conducted controlled detonations of lead azide in Iowa.
The Army performed the controlled detonations at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, after determining that relocating the lead azide could cause an uncontrolled explosion.
The EPA collected post-detonation samples across Iowa, Illinois, and Missouri to monitor potential environmental impacts, and further test results were expected.
body: The Environmental Protection Agency said there was no increase in lead levels in drinking water sources after the Army conducted two controlled detonations of five tons of lead azide in Iowa this week.
The agency’s statement arrived early Saturday morning, nearly three days after the detonations.

“At the time of this press release, initial lab results from EPA’s post-detonation sampling show that the controlled detonation did not result in an elevation of lead in water bodies that serve as sources of drinking water,” the EPA said , adding it “found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake.”
Iowa was the state primarily affected, while nearby Illinois and Missouri were monitored for potential plume drift and fallout.
The EPA disclosed that it sampled 35 drinking water sources across the three states to set a baseline for lead levels before the controlled detonations.

“Though none of these locations were within the area that the plume actually traveled, and all samples were from untreated source water, EPA is sharing the data publicly to ensure transparency,” the agency said.

The operation took place at 9 a.m. local time Wednesday at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, after the military discovered that relocating 68 barrels of lead azide, which is used to make explosives, could have resulted in an uncontrolled explosion. The controlled detonations went smoothly, causing the Trump administration to hail the operation’s success.

White House chief of staff Stephen Miller “convened a historic, all-of-government response to ensure any and all mitigation efforts were deployed to keep everyone safe,” White House communications director Steven Cheung previously posted on X . “It was a spectacular effort by the Administration.”
EPA ANNOUNCES COLLECTION OF OVER 1,000 POST-DETONATION SAMPLES IN IOWA, RESULTS EXPECTED FRIDAY
Cheung reposted the EPA press release and a Fox News interview with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin on the latest update.

“Instead of a spontaneous detonation where everything goes up in the air, you had this perfectly inward detonation where it was driven downwards instead of up into the air. So that was something that the Department of War was very pleased with,” Zeldin said , adding that it was an “all-hands-on-deck effort” from the administration to execute the mitigated blasts and monitor their effects on the environment.

articles.headline: These Galaxy Z Fold 8 Tweaks Will Help You Take Full Advantage of Its 2 Screens
keyFacts: CNET reported that users can customize the Galaxy Z Fold 8 cover screen layout by installing Samsung's Good Lock app and the Home Up plugin.
The reviewer stated that installing the One Hand Operation Plus plugin allows users to add gesture shortcuts for easier one-handed control.
The article noted that users can improve the phone's digital zoom and photo details by adjusting settings within the Camera Assistant.
body: I’ve used and reviewed at least a dozen phones this year, but I keep coming back to the Galaxy Z Fold 8. This foldable phone brings me a strange sense of joy that hasn’t diminished even a few months after its launch (and despite the arrival of a popular rival). I like its symmetrical, thin and lightweight design, but it’s the customizable software experience that’s kept me hooked.

Out of the box, the Galaxy Z Fold 8, like other phones, is quite rigid software-wise. The home screen layout on the cover display is locked to a four-column grid, its camera settings aren’t configured to maximize their potential and you might not know about the multitasking improvements.
Thankfully, you can change these settings, but you’ll need to dive into a few additional tools beyond just the standard Settings menu to do so.
More from CNET

I spent two hours setting up my new Samsung foldable. The process involved installing a couple of apps, changing a few settings and adding new Good Lock plugins. If you’re buying a Galaxy Z Fold 8 this holiday season or have had it for a while, I recommend these changes for a finer, more reliable and personalized experience.
Install the Good Lock app

Good Lock is a Samsung app made for Galaxy phones. You can download it through the Galaxy Store. It’s the first app I install on a Samsung flagship device because it offers customization options that aren’t available by default. For the Galaxy Z Fold 8, I want to highlight two plugins: Home Up and One Hand Operation Plus.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s cover screen doesn’t allow a five-column grid and wastes a lot of space on the home screen. You can’t go past the four-column layout, even if you reduce the icon size (its default icon size is too large for my liking).

If you want a more efficient use of this space, I recommend downloading the Home Up plugin through the Good Lock app (you can easily locate it under the Plugins tab). It lets you change this layout and place icons anywhere you want. You can add up to seven apps in a row or column for a 7-by-7 layout.

I installed it so I could place all my most-used apps and folders on the right side of the home screen for easy one-tap access. I can reach these apps without readjusting my grip. The layout also looks cleaner and more organized. You can perform similar changes to the app drawer by going to the Good Lock app > Home Up > Home screen > Apps list cover column.
Put an end to finger gymnastics

One-hand use is my top priority, and the Fold 8’s wide design isn’t the most ergonomic for system UI elements located on the left side or at the top of the screen. For example, when I need to pull down the Quick Settings Panel, I have to swipe down from the top (I’ve set the pull-down gesture on the home screen to open the Notifications panel). I don’t like readjusting my grip every time I need to adjust a “quick” setting. That’s why I installed One Hand Operation Plus and recommend you do the same.

This Good Lock plugin allows you to add gesture handles to the left and right sides of the screen. You can even reprogram Android’s default swipe back gesture. One Hand Operation Plus lets you add up to six shortcuts within the Short swipe and Long swipe gestures. You can choose from Straight, Diagonal up and Diagonal down swipes.

For my use, I have set the diagonal swipe down from the right side to open the Quick Settings panel. This is a minor change that you’ll appreciate in the long run. Day in and day out, when I need to access Quick Settings, it is no different than swiping down on the home screen to access the Notifications panel. I’ve also set a diagonal swipe up to open the Calculator app because I use it often.

You can also add more functionality with a Long swipe gesture. For instance, a Diagonal down swipe could open the Quick Settings panel, while a long Diagonal down swipe could open a specific setting or app. Samsung also lets you fine-tune the touch area by adjusting the Width, Size and Position.
The Camera Assistant is a must-have

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 cameras aren’t as versatile as the less-expensive Galaxy S26 Ultra’s or the ones found in its more expensive Fold 8 Ultra sibling. It lacks a telephoto lens for optical zoom, so you can’t take sharp photos at 3x or 5x zoom. Instead, the phone’s digital zoom crops into the image captured by the 50-megapixel wide camera. However, you can improve the digital zoom results by changing a few settings within the Camera app.

The Samsung Camera Assistant might be mistaken for a pro feature, but it isn’t. I recommend installing this on every Galaxy flagship phone to get the best output from their camera sensors. To find these hidden settings, you need to go to the Camera app and tap the four-dot menu. Then go to Settings > Camera Assistant > Install.

The very first setting you need to change is the resolution. The Fold 8 has two 50-megapixel cameras but its default resolution is set at 12 megapixels, presumably to save space. I recommend changing it to 24 megapixels for more detailed shots and improved results in 2x as well as 4x zoom. You can do so by going to the Camera settings and then:
- Scroll down to find Camera Assistant. Tap on it.
- Go to Photos settings.
- Tap on 24MP resolution.
- Toggle on two settings here: 24 MP in Photo mode and Keep 24 MP resolution.
While you’re at it, I also recommend adding a 2x zoom shortcut in the viewfinder. Open the Camera Assistant again and turn on the very first setting: 2x crop zoom shortcut.

I often use the 50-megapixel mode, but setting the default resolution to 24 megapixels is the most efficient way to get better-quality photos. It gives you sharper photos with better clarity (at both 1x and 0.6x zoom) without taking up as much storage as the 50-megapixel mode. For the best quality at 4x zoom, I recommend changing the resolution to 50 megapixels so you can get photos like those I embedded from Instagram.
A more intuitive multitasking experience is waiting for you

This isn’t an additional app, but something you should be aware of on the Galaxy Z Fold 8. Samsung improved the multitasking experience on its 2026 foldable lineup. The Fold 8 series allows you to use the split-screen mode in a 90:10 split. It comes in handy when I’m typing in a Google Doc but need to keep my research material visible at a glance.
This is much more intuitive than a 50:50 split because I can, at any given moment, expand one app and trigger the on-screen keyboard comfortably without exiting the split-screen mode.

It is also more intuitive to drag and drop apps in a multitasking mode. You need to go to the Recents menu (swipe up and hold on the home screen), tap and hold the app and drop it on either half of the screen or use it as a pop-up app. The Recents menu then remembers your app grouping for easy access. For instance, if I add Chrome and Google Docs to a split-screen layout and then move to watch Reels on Instagram, I can move back to the split-screen mode by simply going to the Recents menu and tapping on the app group.

articles.headline: 2026 Kindle Paperwhite review: Page-turn buttons are back, for a price
keyFacts: Amazon released the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition priced at $250, featuring an aluminum case and the return of page-turn buttons.
The new 2026 Paperwhite models lack notable screen, lighting, or speed upgrade highlights compared to previous versions, while wireless charging was removed.
Broader tech price increases driven by inflation have pushed the cost of Amazon Kindles and other basic gadgets upward over recent years.
body: Supply pressures, shortages, and inflation have pushed tech prices relentlessly upward over the last half-decade, and even basic gadgets haven’t been immune. That’s why you can spend $385 on a Raspberry Pi, or why the cheapest Amazon Kindle in 2026 costs more than the midrange one from a few years ago. “New thing, better features, same price” used to be a reliable formula, but now you’re lucky if you can get the same thing for barely more than before.

The 2024 Kindles all came with small price increases, but the 2026 models make them look like stellar deals. The $160 Kindle Paperwhite from two years ago wipes the floor with this year’s $150 Kindle in just about every conceivable way, from screen size to front light quality to waterproofing—something to consider if you’re choosing between a used or refurbished Paperwhite and one of these new models.

The flagship of the now five-model-large monochrome Kindle family is the $250 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition, which takes the core specs of the new $200 Paperwhite and puts it in a sturdy iPad-esque aluminum case instead of the typical plastic.

It’s an exceptionally nice reader, and if you’re down with paying even more for it, longtime page-turn button holdouts can recover their precious buttons while still getting the benefits of new, fast Kindle hardware. With the exception of one regression—wireless charging, a feature of the 2024 Signature Edition that has been removed here—it’s the fastest and nicest Kindle you can get. It’s mostly the value, or lack thereof, that leaves a bad taste in one’s mouth.
Hardware updates

Unlike the 2021 or 2024 Kindle Paperwhite updates, the 2026 Paperwhite doesn’t include any notable screen or lighting upgrades. Anyone upgrading from a two- or three-generation-old version of the hardware will still get an upgrade, but the 2026 Paperwhite isn’t doing a ton to push the category forward. And while speed increases were front-and-center in Amazon’s promotional material for the 2024 Paperwhite, Amazon isn’t highlighting any particular gains for this year’s Paperwhite (the base Kindle does apparently open books 30 percent faster than the previous-generation Kindle, though).

articles.headline: Is K-pop sensation Katseye over before it began?
keyFacts: All six members of Katseye perform onstage during the 68th Grammy Awards in Los Angeles on February 1, 2026.
| Kevin Winter/Getty Images for the Recording Academy If you have kids in your life, even if you’re just a funcle, there’s a good chance that you’ve heard Katseye’s music.
And maybe you’ve also been asked for concert tickets.
body: All six members of Katseye perform onstage during the 68th Grammy Awards in Los Angeles on February 1, 2026. | Kevin Winter/Getty Images for the Recording Academy
If you have kids in your life, even if you’re just a funcle, there’s a good chance that you’ve heard Katseye’s music. Maybe repeatedly. And maybe you’ve also been asked for concert tickets.
But before the concerts, before the six-member girl group was nominated for Grammys, and before Katseye even had a hit song, its members had fans.

Worldwide audiences were introduced to the aspiring performers via an American Idol -like competition streamed on YouTube called The Debut: Dream Academy . Over the course of 12 weeks and eight episodes, 20 female contestants competed by completing “missions” that tested their abilities. And viewers voted for their favorites as the competition narrowed down from 20 to 10 and eventually six.

Then came Netflix’s Pop Star Academy: Katseye , which offered viewers a closer behind-the-scenes look at the training, friendships, and tensions from the YouTube competition (including an ongoing feud over effort and attendance among he final six).
By the time listeners finally encountered Katseye’s music, in other words, some watchers had already spent months following the stories of individual members and rooting for them to make the group.

This project was helmed by Hybe , the South Korean company behind BTS , and the American label Geffen . The ambition was global. They wanted women from different countries, trained through the K-pop system, to be launched into the American market, becoming pop stars together.

And for a little while, that experiment seemed to pay off. Katseye landed a viral Gap campaign and a Grammy nomination for Best New Artist , and they also performed at the ceremony. Their rise offered a glimpse of what the American and Korean music industries could build together.

But a series of health-related absences and disrupted performances have raised questions about the group’s future. It has also revived a much older question about pop stardom: How should young artists balance the push to become the next big thing with their own well being?

Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with the pop music journalist Brittany Spanos about Katseye’s difficult year, the limits of what people outside of the Hybe/Geffen leadership know about the recent issues, and the professional pressures of pop stardom that’s familiar to generations of young performers.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .

Katseye performs at the Grammys. They’re part of this huge new artist medley. It’s a lot of eyes on the group. The next big event for them is meant to be Coachella. Does everything look good leading up to that huge moment for them?

This is the part where things start to break down a little bit for Katseye. And I think also reels in a much larger audience than they had hoped into kind of caring about and paying attention to them, which is that Katseye member Manon Bannerman, who hails from Switzerland, ended up going on hiatus from the group.
That was, of course, a pretty big blow for this six-piece group where all the fans have these very deep relationships with each of them — to lose one of their members.
Do we know what happened to Manon?

This is the part where everything gets a little bit tricky with Katseye. There are not really a lot of answers about the hiatus or why she’s on it, whose idea it was, and also if she’ll ever come back, which has led to a lot of speculation about really major drama behind the scenes.

With someone like Manon, there was already a lot of drama lurking beneath the surface with her and the other girls auditioning for Katseye. There were allegations and complaints from other girls who felt like she wasn’t pulling her weight; she took a lot of days off. There was already a bit of that lore kind of hovering over Katseye as they formed and clearly reached a bit of a breaking point in ways that we still don’t really know or understand.
Rough. Do they pull out of Coachella because they lost a member or do they just go through with it?
They do not pull out of Coachella. They end up doing it and they continue on as a five-piece group for the time being.
So you play the Grammys, you play Coachella, then what? You’re supposed to become like the biggest girl group in the world?

They end up going on as planned. They released their single “ Pinky Up ,” and that video does not feature Manon; still no answers on what’s happening with her. But they continue to do their promotional duties and they end up launching an EP called Wild .

But in early August, Katseye member Sophia, who, in a lot of K-pop groups there’s a designated leader. I would say Katseye sort of straddles the line of K-pop structure with a more Western pop group ethos. But Sophia was the designated group leader and she ended up also going on hiatus from the group, leaving them with only four members. And I believe the new date for her return is early next year.
“It does seem to be that there is this desire to capitalize on this moment and keep pushing forward because Katseye is just at the precipice of being extremely huge.”
So this group of six is down to four before they even put out their first album.
Yes.

And, you know, even before they do their headlining tour, which ends up kicking off as scheduled in September, but they were meant to play Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival. And the day before, Katseye member Megan sprains her ankle in tour rehearsals and therefore Katseye pulls out of Daisy Chain Fields , which would have been a pretty big moment for them as well.

Soon after that, they end up going with the tour as planned. And Megan is at the tour at the beginning, but just a couple weeks ago, she had a concussion that led to some canceled tour dates. But they returned to the stage last week. Megan performed in a chair with protective sunglasses on.
This is what caught our attention here at Today, Explained , because you don’t see this every day.
You really don’t.

It really screams like we need an intervention here for this girl group. And we should remind people that to date, this is a group that has not put out an album, which is typically how you engage fans.
They do have three EPs.
Okay. Right. Three EPs. Are people losing the plot here with this group that has this host of issues and no album?

It seems like a very complicated issue, which I can understand with any type of pop group and especially pop groups today. There’s the relationship you have with the group itself and there’s a relationship you have with the individual members of the group as well. In K-pop, they call it biases, where you have one member in particular that you love the most.

I think with each of them, it’s been levels of concern and alarm. When Manon went on hiatus , she’s the only Black member of the group and was being called “lazy” the entire time she was in Dream Academy. And so there are a lot of the racial elements of young Black girls watching this happen and watching this girl be told that she’s not doing enough as the other counterparts in the group, and now all of a sudden, being on a mystery hiatus that no one has explained.

I think Sophia, being the most enthusiastic and being this group leader, not feeling well enough in her mental health to stay in the group rings a lot of alarm bells and I think caused a lot of concern.

And of course with Megan, these back-to-back physical injuries are ringing even more alarm bells where the fans are very much just like, “We would rather Katseye not go on stage than have someone risk their health to perform for us.”
What does this group’s troubles tell us about the industry?
The trouble has always been that young pop groups have been sort of worked to the bone because of the expiration date. We need to get as much out of them as possible before this whole thing implodes.

This is something that the members of One Direction spoke about a lot, which is that their schedule was they were on tour for nine, 10 months of the year, then they were recording an album or then immediately promoting an album. They had like one month to go back home and then they were gone again.
Yeah. And a member of One Direction is of course now dead.
Yes. And Liam was the one who spoke most directly about a lot of that. He was the one who was very open about how taxing that was on his mental and physical health because they were so young.

It does seem to be that there is this desire to capitalize on this moment and keep pushing forward because Katseye is just at the precipice of being extremely huge. They haven’t had the big hit yet. They haven’t released the album, but an arena headline tour is not nothing. A slot in Coachella is not nothing. A Grammy Best New Artist nomination is not nothing.
Do you think it’s too late, or do you still think they have pop dominations somewhere ahead of them?

I don’t know. There’s still a lot of fan desire to see the original six together. Which is, again, a really big handicap for a new pop group: You already don’t have your original band that people wanted to buy tickets to see and watch perform and buy albums from. That’s going to be a big hurdle for them to overcome.

I think a lot of people are wondering how much longer the other members have in them. They seem to be pretty firmly in this, but it doesn’t really look good unless there are some changes potentially made in how they strategize, how to promote and keep Katseye going.

If that means reconfiguring how they do everything and how they promote them, then potentially they can have a huge moment of coming back that’s really triumphant and can make that debut album worth it and can make their next tour even bigger.

Authorities stated that an investigation into the incident was underway.
body: An explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 10, wounds 110

KABUL, Afghanistan — An explosion at a primary and middle school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar Saturday killed 10 people and wounded another 110, most of them children, officials said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for explosives.

Kunar Culture and Information Director Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.
Interior ministry spokesman Abdul Mateen Qani put the death toll at 10, and said 110 had been wounded.
Footage from a ward in the hospital showed young children, several with bandaged heads and some lying two to a bed.
Noor Rahman, whose home is next door to the school, said he heard the explosion and saw dust rising.

"I ran straight into the dust, our own children were there," he said. "I entered one of the rooms, where there was screaming and shouting. I saw the hand of my niece, she was moving it. I rushed in, cleared away the bricks, and managed to pull her out, along with other injured (people)."
Haji Sulaiman, whose son was wounded in the blast, said he had been on his way to his shop when he heard and saw the explosion.

"Pieces of wood and human flesh were flying everywhere," said Sulaiman, adding that he ran toward the school. "When I arrived, I found children, some were dead, others were drenched in blood, and some rooftops were collapsed, the walls were gone, and nothing remained of the school."
Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10 a.m. at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building, part of which appeared to have collapsed.

Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.
Gemstone mining is on the rise in Kunar, with various companies extracting precious stones which are subsequently sold at auction.
In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital, Kabul, wounded more than 40 children aged between 9 and 14.

articles.headline: How to unlock Second Wind in No Asteroids
keyFacts: Players must acquire an Oxygen Ampoule, which provides 15 extra seconds of air to prevent death when oxygen runs out.
Players need to go outside their pod, ignore the first oxygen warning, and continue mining until their oxygen is completely depleted.
The Second Wind achievement unlocks when the Oxygen Ampoule activates and the player returns to the pod within 15 seconds.
body: Second Wind is one of the trickier achievements to unlock in No Asteroids . Fail to do it properly, and you’ll end up dying in pursuit of the achievement. However, the task isn’t too difficult if you know what needs to be done.
How to complete Second Wind achievement in No Asteroids

The first thing you’ll need is an Oxygen Ampoule. This is an emergency device that saves your life if you run out of air. It gives you a window of 15 seconds with extra air so that you can safely get back to your pod. Without it, you’ll simply collapse if you run out of air.
Screenshot by Destructoid
Next, go outside your pod, and start mining. You’ll observe that your oxygen is running out gradually as you spend more time outside the pod. You’ll get a first warning; ignore that.

You’ll want to continue mining until your oxygen is completely depleted. Thankfully, you have the Oxygen Ampoule and the valuable 15 seconds of air it provides. The Ampoule will activate as soon as your Oxygen reserve is empty.
Once that happens, immediately return to the safety of your pod. You must do this within 15 seconds, so don’t go too far away. This will unlock the Second Wind achievement in No Asteroids.

articles.headline: Zelenskyy questions Trump’s ‘strange’ reference to Putin as a ‘friend’
keyFacts: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized U.S. President Donald Trump for referring to Russian leader Vladimir Putin as a friend.
Trump defended his remarks, stating that his goal is to broker a peace deal to stop the ongoing war in Ukraine.
European Union leaders failed to reach a consensus on a new $49 billion loan for Ukraine.
body: KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington, as new questions emerged about Europe’s future financial commitments to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Trump calling Putin “my friend” at a recent summit in China as “strange” because the Russian leader is “an aggressor and a killer.”
“He can’t be a friend,” Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening the statement to someone calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on Zelenskyy’s remarks. But Trump on Thursday defended his reference to Putin. “We want to make a deal. We want to stop the killing,” he said.

“I could walk in and say, ‘I don’t like you!’ and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelenskyy and Putin,” he said. Speaking to reporters at Mar-a-Lago, he added: “The biggest problem with that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Zelenskyy was “insulting his counterpart,” showing that the Ukrainian leader “is not willing to follow the path of (a) peace settlement.”

The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies, including Israel.
The Kremlin has said that Russia also does not recognize the ICC and considers its decisions “legally void.” Peskov in 2023 called the court’s move against Putin “outrageous and unacceptable.”

Zelenskyy’s comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a “grandmaster” of politics and weeks after Kushner’s partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a “humanitarian.”

Moscow’s invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of troops and thousands of Ukrainian civilians. It also brought heavy sanctions on Russia and diplomatically isolated Putin in the West before Trump resumed relations.

At the same time, Zelenskyy has complained that the Pentagon is not delivering to Ukraine paid-for Patriot missiles that could stop Russia’s ballistic missiles and that SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication, isn’t working properly.

Europe has in the past vowed to stay the course in helping Ukraine fend off Russia’s invasion. But European Union leaders on Thursday failed to reach consensus after fraught talks over a new $49 billion loan for Ukraine’s economic and military needs next year.
Elections in the EU over the next 12 months could amplify the influence of parties reluctant to send more money to Ukraine and may fray the continent’s support.
The grinding aerial bombardment between Russia and Ukraine has escalated recently.

Russia launched close to 300 aerial attacks a week through Nov. 20 on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, or ACLED, which tracks violence.

articles.headline: Pensions and benefits services still down after 'cyber incident'
keyFacts: Online pensions and benefits services remained offline following a cyber incident that the Department for Work and Pensions took precautions to address.
The government stated that regular payments would continue and no personal information was believed to have been lost or stolen.
Authorities are investigating the incident in collaboration with the National Cyber Security Centre.
body: - Published
Online benefits and pensions services were still down on Saturday morning following a "cyber incident" which forced the government to take them offline.
The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has not specified what triggered it to shut down access late on Thursday but has not ruled out that it was hit by hackers.

The government has assured benefits recipients and pensioners that their usual payments would continue to be made, though some people have reported delays and fear being penalised for missing deadlines to report information online.
The UK's former chief technology officer David Knott told BBC Newsnight his "strong suspicion" was that the department had been targeted by hackers.
He continued: "[The government has] taken down some of the citizen-facing services, which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door."

John Curry, a leading cyber security expert based at Bath Spa University, told BBC News the DWP had "almost certainly" detected hacking activity taking place and shut down its systems in an effort to stop data being stolen.
Curry said if the DWP had discovered hackers inside its computer systems, then the "best thing to do is slam the front door shut".

He also said the government may deliberately release limited information in order to "keep the enemy in the dark" and not give any possible hackers hints about ongoing work to secure sensitive systems.

On Friday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said there had been a "serious cyber incident" without offering further details, while the department said the move to close online services was a "precaution".
Downing Street would not be drawn on whether the DWP had been targeted by hackers but did say other departments had not been accessed by a "malicious actor".
The government said it was working with GCHQ's National Cyber Security Centre to investigate the incident, which indicates a hack has not been ruled out.
The DWP makes around 2.5 million payments every day. Online portals for Pip applications and the "Tell Us Once" system for registering deaths have also been impacted.
The government also said on Friday that it did not believe any personal information had been lost or stolen.
The incident has fuelled concerns about the vulnerability of state computer systems and whether security protocols are keeping pace with advances in AI technology, which can be used to aid hackers.
Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the House of Commons Science and Technology Committee, said the DWP incident should be a "wake-up call" for the government.

She continued: "People rely on these systems for some of the most essential services the state provides, and they should be able to trust that the tech and data underpinning them are secure and resilient."

Shadow AI minister Ben Spencer said the DWP incident was "deeply concerning", saying the government cannot "demand higher standards of cyber security from others without demonstrating that government are taking the necessary action to protect their own systems".
It is the latest in a run of global cyber incidents impacting government and major organisations, which have been variously triggered by hackers, faulty tech or botched upgrades.
Additional reporting by Jacob Phillips

articles.headline: Could Donald Trump And Abdul El-Sayed Really Team Up On Universal Healthcare?
keyFacts: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed urged President Donald Trump to embrace a universal healthcare program called TrumpCare, issuing digital golden cards for the initiative.
A White House official dismissed the universal healthcare proposal in an email, citing a Council of Economic Advisers analysis that predicted a large deficit increase.
Democratic leaders are divided on whether to negotiate policy deals with Trump or pass popular legislation knowing he might veto the bills.
body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s second-term obsession with his legacy has led him to seek a vast reshaping of Washington, slapping his name on buildings, remaking the White House in his image and even building a literal monument to himself.

Democrats have vociferously fought most of these efforts. But some in the party are still holding out hope they can use Trump’s desire to etch his name into history to convince him to adopt progressive policy, resurrecting a long-held dream Democrats can exploit a latent progressive streak in the president.

These dreams have almost uniformly ended without real results, with whatever ideological flexibility Trump possesses stomped out by hard-liners on his staff and among Republicans in Congress. But some Democrats insist it might be worth trying anyway.

The highest-profile attempt after the midterm elections is coming from Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), who has used a series of social media posts and interviews to try and impress upon Trump the glory of enacting “Medicare for All,” calling it “TrumpCare” and giving everyone in America a golden TrumpCare card.
“I don’t care whose name’s on it,” El-Sayed said this week. “I just care that people have healthcare.”

“He’s a smart guy,” Trump told the New York Post, only weeks after he headlined a rally where Republicans repeatedly suggested El-Sayed was a terrorist. “He did a good job. He actually did a very good job.”

The president has shared an El-Sayed post about “TrumpCare” on his Truth Social website without comment. But the White House hasn’t signaled any actual openness to the idea, which seems extremely unlikely, considering Trump’s most recent healthcare policies were to cut Medicaid and allow Obamacare subsidies to expire.

Indeed, a White House official panned the idea in an email, pointing to a Council of Economic Advisers analysis that said “Medicare for All” would widen budget deficits by $47 trillion and pay for more than a million gender-affirming surgeries.
“Medicare for All will inevitably increase your taxes,” the official said.
So that’s what they think of that.

Still, El-Sayed’s golden “TrumpCare” cards illustrate a central question confronting Democrats as they prepare to take control of Congress in January: Should they try to cut deals with Trump, or should they pass bills reflecting the popular ideas they campaigned on, even if Trump vetoes everything they send to his desk?
“It’s hard for a president to just spend two years doing nothing but vetoing popular bills.”

The party’s leaders — Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) — have vowed to enact an affordability agenda that, among other things, undoes Trump’s tariffs, reverses his Medicaid cuts, revives Obamacare subsidies and raises the minimum wage, but they haven’t figured out how many individual bills to send or exactly what those bills would look like. One vision calls for lots of little bills that would maximize the political repercussions of a series of unpopular vetoes.

“By moving clear, understandable, important pieces of legislation on a standalone basis, it’s sort of a win-win situation: You either can notch real victories because you get Trump to sign it, or maybe you have to negotiate a little bit and get him to sign a slightly modified version of it, or he vetoes it, and Democrats can say, ‘Look, we passed a major expansion of health insurance, and he vetoed it,’” Bharat Ramamurti, former deputy director of the National Economic Council under President Joe Biden, told HuffPost.

Since 1980, there have been eight instances of one party controlling the House and Senate while the other holds the White House, according to an analysis by Ramamurti. Democratic Congresses have passed significant progressive legislation under Republican presidents, such as a federal minimum wage increase that President George W. Bush signed into law in 2007.

But Ramamurti said Democrats should “play to show” at least as much as they should try to enact merely incremental policy victories. He pointed to a Republican Congress passing welfare reform in the 1990s. President Bill Clinton vetoed two bills before finally signing one into law.

“That can be a template in some ways for getting a president to eventually cave to the political reality, because Congress sets the agenda, and it’s hard for a president to just spend two years doing nothing but vetoing popular bills,” Ramamurti said.
As for Trump: “He’s a very unpredictable guy, and the potential set of outcomes to me seems very broad. And so you might as well try for big-ticket items.”

Since the midterm elections, Trump has threatened to use his veto pen liberally, but he’s also mused occasionally about working with Democrats. He did the same thing in his first term, however, and it never worked out. In 2019, when Democrats controlled the House, he cut a deal with Schumer and then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) for a $2 trillion infrastructure bill, then bailed on the deal a month later because he was mad about Democrats investigating his administration.

Trump has suggested since the election he’d be open to bipartisan immigration reform, acknowledging his deportation policy may have been “too tough,” but it’s another show we’ve seen before. In 2018, Trump invited a bipartisan group of lawmakers to the White House and urged them to write a bill that included a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers. A month later, when the senators unveiled their bill, the White House crapped on it, and it died.
“Trump sent the signal: ‘You guys put a bill on my desk,’” Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), one of the senators involved in the deal, recalled this month in an interview with HuffPost.
“They immediately poured cold water on it,” Kaine said. “Trump did a 180 from what he promised.”
